title: Notation
body_md: Throughout the paper the alphabet indicates the block structure of the objects involved. Roman letters denote operators acting on scalar functions on the interface $\Gamma$ (the Helmholtz boundary integral operators, the tangential derivative, the Hilbert transform, the mean value operator) and $H^s(\Gamma)$ denotes the usual Sobolev spaces. Calligraphic letters denote objects with two components: the product spaces $\mathcal H^s(\Gamma):=H^s(\Gamma)\times H^s(\Gamma)$ and the $2\times2$ block operators acting on them; for a scalar operator $\mathrm A$, the same letter in calligraphic font, $\mathcal A$, denotes its componentwise action. Fraktur letters denote $2\times2$ block operators whose blocks are themselves calligraphic operators, such as the transmission operator $\mathfrak A_\alpha$ and the preconditioners $\mathfrak P^{\rm left}$, $\mathfrak P^{\rm right}$ of Sections~\ref{GradHessCalculations} and~\ref{sec:preconditioning}. Vectors and vector fields are set in bold.

label: theo:transmission:helmholtz
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice first that, as a consequence of \eqref{eq:expansions}, the principal part of ${\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho}$ is given by
  \begin{equation}
 {\cal L}^{\rm p}_{\alpha,\rho}:=
\frac{1}2\begin{bmatrix*}[r]
(1-\alpha)\mathrm{I} &   -(1+\alpha) \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{D}_{-1}+\operatorname{J})\\
(1+\rho \alpha)\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{D} +\operatorname{J}) & (1-\alpha\rho)\operatorname{I}
\end{bmatrix*}. 
\end{equation}
That is, ${\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho}-{\cal L}^{\rm p}_{\alpha,\rho}: H^s(\Gamma)\times H^{s-1}(\Gamma) \to H^s(\Gamma)\times H^{s-1}(\Gamma)$ is compact. Moreover, a direct calculation shows that
\[
   \left({\cal L}^{\rm p}_{\alpha,\rho}\right)^{-1}=
-\frac{1}{\alpha(\rho+1)}  \begin{bmatrix*}[r]
 (1-\alpha\rho)\operatorname{I} &  (1+\alpha ) \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{D}_{-1}+\operatorname{J})\\
 -(1+\rho \alpha)\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{D} +\operatorname{J}) &  (1-\alpha)\mathrm{I}
\end{bmatrix*}.
\]
Therefore, ${\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho}$ is Fredholm of index zero.  

We will prove the injectivity of ${\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho}$ by applying a well-known argument that uses the jump relations for single and double layer potentials and the dual transmission problem. References for such arguments for $\alpha=\pm 1$ can be found in \cite{costabel-stephan,kress1978transmission}. We extend such results to any $\alpha\ne 0$ (and $\rho>0$) for the sake of completeness. Let $(g,\varphi)\in \ker({\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho})$, and define in $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\Gamma$ the fields
\[
u_1:= -{\rm SL}_{k_1}[\varphi] +{\rm DL}_{k_1}[g],\quad  u_2:= \alpha \left( {\rm SL}_{k_2}[\varphi] - {\rm DL}_{k_2}[g]\right). 
\]Since $(g,\varphi)\in \ker({\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho})$, the pair $v_1 := u_1|_{\Omega_1}$, $v_2 := u_2|_{\Omega_2}$ solves the homogeneous transmission problem
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trhelmholt:01}
 \left\{
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \Delta v_1 + k_1^2 v_1 = 0, & \text{in } \Omega_1,\\
 \Delta v_2 + k_2^2 v_2 = 0, & \text{in } \Omega_2,\\
 \gamma^{(1)} v_1 - \gamma^{(2)} v_2 =  0, & \\
 \partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} v_1 -  \rho\, \partial_{\bm n}^{(2)} v_2 = 0, & \\
 \partial_{\bm r} v_1 - i k_1 v_1 = o(r^{-1/2}), &
 \end{array}
 \right.
\end{equation}
which is well posed. Hence $u_1=0$ in $\Omega_1$ and $u_2=0$ in $\Omega_2$, and the jump relations \eqref{eq:traces} yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \gamma^{(2)} u_1 &= -\big(\gamma^{(1)} u_1-\gamma^{(2)} u_1\big) = -g, &
 \partial_{\bm n}^{(2)} u_1 &= -\big(\partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} u_1-\partial_{\bm n}^{(2)} u_1\big) = -\varphi,\\
 \gamma^{(1)} u_2 &= \gamma^{(1)} u_2-\gamma^{(2)} u_2 = -\alpha g, &
 \partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} u_2 &= \partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} u_2-\partial_{\bm n}^{(2)} u_2 = -\alpha\varphi .
 \end{aligned}
\]
That is, the Cauchy data of $u_2|_{\Omega_1}$ are $\alpha$ times those of $u_1|_{\Omega_2}$, so that, by Green's formula in $\Omega_2$,
\[
 \int_{\Gamma} \partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} u_2\, \overline{u_2}
 = |\alpha|^2 \int_{\Gamma} \partial_{\bm n}^{(2)} u_1\, \overline{u_1}
 = |\alpha|^2\Big(\int_{\Omega_2}|\nabla u_1|^2 - k_1^2 \int_{\Omega_2}| u_1|^2\Big)\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Since $u_2|_{\Omega_1}$ is a radiating solution of the Helmholtz equation with wavenumber $k_2$, applying Green's formula again, now in the intersection of $\Omega_1$ with the ball $B({\bf 0},R)$ for $R$ large enough, we obtain
\[
0=\Im \int_{\Gamma} \partial_{\bm n}^{(1)} u_2\, \overline{u_2}=\lim_{R\to \infty}
\Im  \int_{|{\bf x}|=R} \partial_{\bm r} u_2\, {\overline{u_2}}=k_2\lim_{R\to \infty}
 \int_{|{\bf x}|=R} |u_2|^2.
\]
Rellich's lemma (cf. \cite[Lemma 3.3.2]{SaVa:2002} or \cite[Lemma 2.12]{ColtonKress}) implies $u_2=0$ in $\Omega_1$. Therefore $g=-\alpha^{-1}\gamma^{(1)}u_2=0$ and $\varphi=-\alpha^{-1}\partial_{\bm n}^{(1)}u_2=0$, which proves the injectivity of ${\cal L}_{\alpha,\rho}$ and therefore its invertibility.

label: theo:unicity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theo:unicity}
Equation \eqref{eq:cfie_t} admits at most  one solution for any $\alpha\ne 0$ and $\rho> 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $({\bm \varphi},{\bm g})$ be a solution of \eqref{eq:cfie_t} with homogeneous data, and let $u^{(p)}_j$ and $u^{(s)}_j$ be defined by \eqref{eq:representation}. By uniqueness of the transmission problem, we have
\[
\nabla u^{(p)}_j + \operatorname{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{curl}}} u^{(s)}_j = {\bf 0},
\qquad \text{in } \Omega_j, \quad j=1,2.
\]
Taking the divergence, we obtain
\[
\Delta u^{(p)}_j
=
\operatorname{div}\big(\nabla u^{(p)}_j + \operatorname{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{curl}}} u^{(s)}_j\big)
=0,\quad \text{in } \Omega_j, \quad j=1,2.
\]
Since $u^{(p)}_j$ also satisfies the Helmholtz equation in $\Omega_j$, it follows that actually $u^{(p)}_j=0$ in $\Omega_j$. 

Hence the Cauchy data of $u^{(p)}_1$ and $u^{(p)}_2$ on $\Gamma$ vanish and, by \eqref{eq:representation:a}, the pair $(g^{(p)},\varphi^{(p)})$ solves the homogeneous system of BIEs
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lformulation:principal:part}
\frac{1}2 \begin{bmatrix}
(1-\alpha)g^{(p)}\\
(1-\alpha\rho )\varphi^{(p)}\\
\end{bmatrix} +\begin{bmatrix}
{\rm K}_{p_1}+\alpha {\rm K}_{p_2} & -{\rm V}_{p_1}-\alpha {\rm V}_{p_2}\\
{\rm W}_{p_1}+\alpha\rho {\rm W}_{p_2} & -{\rm K}^\top_{p_1}-\alpha  \rho{\rm K}^\top_{p_2}\\
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
g^{(p)}\\
\varphi^{(p)}\\
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}
  0\\
  0
\end{bmatrix},
\end{equation}
which is \eqref{eq:Lformulation} with $k_j=k_p^{(j)}$.
By Theorem \ref{theo:transmission:helmholtz}, this system is uniquely solvable, which implies that $g^{(p)}=\varphi^{(p)}=0$.
 


The argument for $u_j^{(s)}$ is analogous. Indeed, taking the curl in
\[
\nabla u^{(p)}_j + \operatorname{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{curl}}} u^{(s)}_j = {\bf 0},
\]
we deduce
\[
0=\operatorname{curl}\big(\nabla u^{(p)}_j + \operatorname{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{curl}}} u^{(s)}_j\big) = -\Delta u^{(s)}_j.
\]
Since $u^{(s)}_j$ also satisfies the Helmholtz equation in $\Omega_j$, we conclude that $u^{(s)}_j=0$ in $\Omega_j$. Repeating the same argument as above for the shear wave component, we obtain $\varphi^{(s)}=0$ and $g^{(s)}=0$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{p},\alpha}$ be the principal part of
$\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}:\mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s+1}(\Gamma) \to \mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s-1}(\Gamma)$.
Then, the kernel of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{p},\alpha}$ is given by
\[
\left\{ (-(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f,0,0,f)^\top + (0,(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})g,g,0)^\top \ :\ f,g \in H^{s+1}(\Gamma) \right\}
\subset \mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s+1}(\Gamma),
\]
and is therefore independent of the choice of $\alpha$ and $\rho$. In particular, $\ker(\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{p},\alpha})$ is infinite-dimensional.

Furthermore, the cokernel of $\mathfrak{A}_{\mathrm{p},\alpha}$ is also infinite-dimensional, although it depends on the choice of $\alpha$ and $\rho$.

Consequently, $\mathfrak{A}_{\alpha}:\mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s+1}(\Gamma) \to \mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s-1}(\Gamma)$ is not a Fredholm operator.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is easy to check that for any $f,g \in H^{s+1}(\Gamma)$, we have
\[
(-(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f,0,0,f)^\top, \quad
(0,(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})g,g,0)^\top
\in\ker(\mathfrak{A}_{\rm p}^{(j)}), \quad j=1,2.
\]
Now, let $(\bm{\varphi},\bm{g}) \in \mathcal{H}^{s}(\Gamma)\times \mathcal{H}^{s+1}(\Gamma)$ be an arbitrary element, which can be written as
\[
(\bm{\varphi},\bm{g}) = (-(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f_1, ( \mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f_2, f_3, f_4)^\top, \quad f_i \in H^{s+1}(\Gamma).
\]
Notice that we can decompose it as
\[
(\bm{\varphi},\bm{g}) = (-(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f_1,0,0,f_1)^\top + (0,(\mathrm{D} + \operatorname{J})f_2,f_2,0)^\top + (0,0,f_3-f_2,f_4-f_1)^\top.
\]
Since the first two terms belong to the kernel of $\mathfrak{A}_{\rm p}^{(j)}$, we have that $(\bm{\varphi},\bm{g}) \in \ker(\mathfrak{A}_{\rm p,\alpha})$ if and only if (cf. \eqref{eq:Hinvbeta})
\[
(f_3-f_2, f_4-f_1)^\top \in \ker(\mathcal{H}_{(1,-1)} + \alpha \mathcal{H}_{(1,1)})\cap\ker(\mathcal{H}_{(1,-1)} - r \mathcal{H}_{(1,1)}), \quad r = \alpha\rho \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} \ne 0,
\]
the two conditions coming from the first and second block rows of $\mathfrak{A}_{\rm p,\alpha}$, respectively. Since $\mathcal{H}_{(1,-1)} + \alpha \mathcal{H}_{(1,1)}=\mathcal{H}_{(1+\alpha,-1+\alpha)}$ is invertible by \eqref{eq:Hinvbeta} ($(1+\alpha)^2-(\alpha-1)^2=4\alpha\ne0$), we conclude that $f_3=f_2$ and $f_4=f_1$, which proves the first part.

For the cokernel, one checks in the same way that the range of $\mathfrak{A}_{\rm p,\alpha}$ is the graph of a bounded operator over two of the four components, so that it has infinite codimension; its description depends on $\alpha$, $\rho$, $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$ and we omit it.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have already shown that $\mathfrak P^{\rm left}\mathfrak A_\alpha\mathfrak A_1^{\rm right}\mathfrak A_2^{\rm right}$ is a compact perturbation of the identity, and $\mathfrak P^{\rm right}$ differs from $\mathfrak A_1^{\rm right}\mathfrak A_2^{\rm right}$ by a smoothing operator. Hence, \eqref{eq:01:theo:01} is proven.
  
  Furthermore, $\mathfrak{P}^{\rm right}$  is invertible, in particular injective.  On the other hand,   $\mathfrak{P}^{\rm left}$ is injective if so are
 $\mathfrak{A}^{\rm left}_{2}:{\cal H}^s(\Gamma)\times {\cal H}^s(\Gamma)\to {\cal H}^s(\Gamma)\times {\cal H}^s(\Gamma)$ and ${\cal S}_{21}:{\cal H}^s(\Gamma)\to {\cal H}^s(\Gamma)$ in \eqref{eq:S21}.  For the former, the diagonal blocks are
\begin{align*}
    {\frac{1}2 \mathcal{H}_{(1,1)}-\frac{1}{2\alpha} \mathcal{H}_{(1, -1)} } &=
    \frac1{2\alpha}\mathcal{H}_{(\alpha-1, \alpha+1)},\\
\frac{1}{4\alpha\rho\mu_1\mu_2}
\left(
\mu_1 \mathcal H_{(1,-1)}
+
\alpha\rho\mu_2 \mathcal H_{(1,1)}\right) &=
\frac{1}{4\alpha\rho\mu_1\mu_2}\mathcal H_{(\alpha\rho\mu_2+\mu_1,\alpha\rho\mu_2-\mu_1)},
\end{align*}
which are invertible by \eqref{eq:Hinvbeta}, since 
\[
(\alpha-1)^2-(\alpha+1)^2=-4\alpha\ne0, \quad (\alpha\rho\mu_2+\mu_1)^2-(\alpha\rho\mu_2-\mu_1)^2=4\alpha\rho\mu_1\mu_2\ne0.
\]

On the other hand, the eigenvalues of ${\cal S}_{21}$ are $2\sigma$ and $2\zeta$, so that ${\cal S}_{21}$ is injective if
 \[
\sigma,\zeta\ne 0.
\]
But, using \eqref{eq:ks:kp}, we have
\[
\sigma = \frac{\omega^2}{\lambda_1+2\mu_1}\Big[(\lambda_1+\mu_1)(\mu_1+\mu_2\rho)+2\mu_1\mu_2\rho\Big],\qquad
\zeta  = \frac{\alpha^2\rho\,\omega^2}{\lambda_2+2\mu_2}\Big[(\lambda_2+\mu_2)(\mu_1+\mu_2\rho)+2\mu_1\mu_2\Big],
\]
which are strictly positive since $\mu_j,\rho>0$, $\lambda_j+\mu_j>0$ and $\alpha\ne0$. Hence $\mathcal S_{21}$ is invertible.  

Since $\mathfrak P^{\rm left}$ and $\mathfrak P^{\rm right}$ are injective, Theorem \ref{theo:unicity} implies that $\mathfrak P^{\rm left}\mathfrak A_\alpha\mathfrak P^{\rm right}$ is injective, and by the Fredholm alternative it is invertible, which finishes the proof.
